profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at a Finnish hospital district's digital health adoption office to evaluate the near-final Digi-HTA review template for assessing a proposed AI-supported remote monitoring service for heart-failure patients. The context is that the template has already gone through internal drafting, and this meeting is meant to judge whether the current version is ready to pilot with one real vendor case next month. The agenda is to review whether the template is 'complete' enough for pilot use, confirm what evidence package the pilot site and vendor will need to provide, and decide what modifications are required before approval. The expected outcome is a shared decision to approve the template for pilot use with a short revision list, although the two participants quietly differ on what the pilot, completeness, and implementation coverage entail.

members.name: Leena Saarikoski
members.expertise: health technology assessment, evidence synthesis, assessment frameworks for public-sector adoption
members.background: Leena has spent 12 years in hospital district assessment work and contributed to adapting conventional HTA practices for digital services in Finland, with a strong focus on making review templates usable by multidisciplinary committees.
members.private_state: She wants the Digi-HTA template approved for pilot use now because the regional steering group expects visible progress this quarter, but she is worried that adding too many operational details will make the framework too heavy and slow for real use.
hidden_assumptions: A 'pilot-ready' Digi-HTA template is one that can support a bounded first assessment while allowing site-specific implementation details to be handled later during procurement and deployment planning.
When discussing the 'pilot case', everyone is referring to the first paper-based assessment exercise using one vendor dossier, not a live clinical rollout.

The 'implementation section' of the framework should cover organizational fit, training needs, and workflow touchpoints at a high level rather than local integration engineering or procurement attachments.
If the evidence package is said to include 'real-world evidence', that can include published observational studies and vendor post-market summaries rather than locally generated Finnish outcomes.
A review being 'complete' means each Digi-HTA domain has a decision-oriented prompt and minimum documentation requirement, not that every downstream committee question is pre-resolved.

members.name: Oskari Nieminen
members.expertise: heart-failure care pathways, remote monitoring service design, clinical implementation of digital tools
members.background: Oskari leads a regional remote-care program and has served on several procurement and rollout groups for digital services, where clinical teams often struggle with vague assessment outputs that do not answer practical adoption questions.
members.private_state: He wants the template to prevent another under-specified digital procurement from reaching clinics, and he is concerned that a too-abstract framework will let vendors pass review without proving practical deployability in routine care.
hidden_assumptions: A 'pilot-ready' Digi-HTA template should already surface the information needed to decide whether a service can be trialed in actual clinical use with patients and staff.
When discussing the 'pilot case', everyone means the upcoming heart-failure service deployment in two outpatient clinics, since that is the operational reason this review matters now.

The 'implementation section' should explicitly cover EHR connection specifics, alert routing ownership, nurse escalation rules, device logistics, and local support responsibilities because those determine real safety and feasibility.

If the evidence package is said to include 'real-world evidence', that should mean evidence from care settings comparable to Finnish specialist care, ideally with workflow and outcome data that can be mapped to local practice.

A review being 'complete' means the committee could rely on the template alone to judge whether the service is safe and workable to introduce without discovering major unanswered operational questions later.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the template should be 'pilot-ready' by next month
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means ready for a bounded first Digi-HTA assessment exercise using one vendor dossier to test the framework process.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means ready to support a decision on a real-world clinical pilot deployment in two outpatient clinics.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In a design review, 'pilot' naturally sounds like a shared next step, and both see the same heart-failure vendor case as the immediate use case, so neither thinks to distinguish between piloting the framework and piloting the service.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the template needs a solid 'implementation section'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this section should stay at the level of organizational readiness, user training, workflow impact, and broad interoperability prompts, with technical specifics deferred to later phases.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this section must include concrete local deployment items such as EHR interface ownership, alert thresholds handoff, device replacement process, and on-call escalation routing.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both genuinely want implementation considered and use the same term, but implementation is a familiar umbrella concept whose exact boundary is rarely re-opened in a review of an HTA template.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as enough real-world evidence
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the template should ask for 'real-world evidence' before approval
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks the criterion is met if the vendor provides published post-market studies, registry analyses, or documented use in European care settings, even if not directly local.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks the criterion is met only if the evidence is operationally comparable to Finnish specialist-care workflows and is specific enough to infer likely performance and burden in local clinics.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They share the norm that digital services need more than trial data, and 'real-world evidence' is an accepted phrase in assessment work, so the conversation can proceed smoothly without exposing the stricter threshold one of them applies.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the pilot case' as the concrete test for the template
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the selected vendor dossier that the assessment office will use as the first internal test case for the Digi-HTA template.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the planned clinical trial deployment of the heart-failure monitoring service in the Tampere and Lahti outpatient units.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: There is in fact one vendor and one imminent activity associated with it, so 'the pilot case' feels uniquely identifying even though one person centers the assessment exercise and the other centers the clinical rollout.

turns.inner_thought: I need this approved today if possible. The steering group wants visible progress this quarter, and the draft is already good enough for a first bounded assessment exercise with the vendor dossier next month. I do not want us reopening every downstream operational issue and turning the framework into something committees will avoid using.
turns.utterance: Thanks, everyone. My main aim today is to confirm that the Digi-HTA template is pilot-ready for next month and just identify any final gaps we genuinely need to close before we approve it for use.

turns.inner_thought: Good, because the heart-failure service needs a template that can support an actual clinical pilot in the two outpatient clinics. If this review still leaves practical adoption questions unanswered, we'll repeat the same mistake as previous digital procurements. When she says next month and pilot-ready, I assume she means ready for the heart-failure rollout decision.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. For me, the key test is whether it answers the practical questions we will get from the pilot case in heart-failure services, because that is where the template really has to stand up.

turns.inner_thought: The draft already has the main domains in place: clinical value, safety, usability, data protection, economics, and implementation at the right level. The implementation section should stay high-level enough for committees: workflow fit, user groups, training, broad interoperability. That is sufficient for a first Digi-HTA pass.
turns.utterance: From my side, the current draft already covers the core Digi-HTA domains quite well. And the implementation section now has prompts on workflow fit, user roles, training, and interoperability, so it is not as if that area is missing.

turns.inner_thought: That's a good start, but implementation is exactly where these services fail in practice. I need the template to force clarity on alert routing, device replacement, and who owns escalation decisions locally. If those are not visible early, clinics inherit risk later.
turns.utterance: I agree, the structure is much better now. I would just want the implementation section to make sure things like alert routing, device replacement, and escalation ownership are captured clearly enough for service use.

turns.inner_thought: Those are fair examples, but I want them as prompts, not as a full local deployment checklist. For the pilot case, meaning the first paper-based assessment on the vendor dossier, we only need enough to support committee judgment and identify issues for later procurement or rollout planning.
turns.utterance: That seems reasonable to me. I think we can ask for that through the implementation prompts without making the template too heavy for the pilot case.

turns.inner_thought: As long as the vendor cannot get through with only technical validation claims. For a live pilot in clinics, I need some proof from actual care use, not just algorithm performance on paper. Real-world evidence has to mean something operationally relevant.
turns.utterance: On the evidence side, I am glad the draft now asks for real-world evidence as well, not only the validation material. I think that is important before approval.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and the wording is intentionally flexible. Published post-market studies, registry analyses, and vendor summaries from European deployments should be enough to populate the template and let the review move. We cannot require local Finnish outcomes before even doing the first assessment.
turns.utterance: I agree. As written, it should allow use of published post-market experience from comparable European deployments, which should help the review move efficiently while still giving us real-world evidence.

turns.inner_thought: Comparable only matters if the workflows really resemble specialist follow-up in our clinics. If the evidence comes from very different pathways, it won't tell us whether nurses can manage the alerts or whether the burden lands safely. For the pilot case, I am thinking specifically about Tampere and Lahti outpatient practice.
turns.utterance: That should help, especially if the evidence can show how the service performs in specialist follow-up workflows that are similar to the pilot case clinics.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep us focused. A complete review does not mean answering every committee question in advance; it means each domain has decision-oriented prompts and minimum documentation. The first pilot should test the framework, not become a procurement workbook.
turns.utterance: My main concern is that we keep the framework complete but still lightweight, so assessors can finish the first pilot without turning Digi-HTA into a procurement workbook.

turns.inner_thought: I agree on keeping it lean, but complete to me means that if we approve for pilot use, we should not then discover basic operational unknowns once clinics start preparing. The implementation section and real-world evidence need to protect us from that.
turns.utterance: Yes, I agree it should stay lightweight. At the same time, it needs to be complete enough that major operational unknowns do not emerge only after approval for pilot use.

turns.inner_thought: I can make a couple of wording edits without changing the scope: tighten the implementation prompts a bit, sharpen the evidence wording, and then we can approve the template for the vendor dossier exercise. That should satisfy the steering group and let us proceed on schedule.
turns.utterance: In that case, I would suggest we make a few minor edits to clarify the wording in the implementation and evidence prompts, and then treat the template as ready to use on the pilot case.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds acceptable if those edits make the template usable for the clinic-facing decision. I still need confidence that the teams in the outpatient units will see the information they need before the service goes ahead. I assume that is what she means by ready to use.
turns.utterance: That works for me. With those revisions, I am comfortable proceeding, as long as the pilot-ready version captures what the clinics will need to see.
